extracted.intended_audience: students learning news writing / journalism students and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and analytic checklist for writing and analyzing newspaper news and feature stories, covering types, structure, style, sourcing, purpose, and typographical conventions. Intended as a textbook chapter for journalism instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of story — informative vs feature
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two general types of news stories: (1) the informative news story, the chief aim of which is to give the facts of the news; and (2) the feature or human interest story, the chief aim of which is to take material of little or no news value and make it interesting. The fundamental difference ... is the news value of the contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informative stories prioritize news value; feature stories prioritize interest and literary skill. Human-interest elements can appear in informative pieces. Length and lead style follow the story type (summary lead for informative; fiction-style openings for features).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informative story subtypes — purely informative and constructive
rubrics_metrics.description: The informative news story may be (1) the story whose chief purpose is to record the facts without particular regard to effect on readers; and (2) the story that presents facts so as to produce a wholesome (constructive) effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purely informative aims for rapid-grasp facts and usually a summary lead; constructive informative aims to interest readers in significance, may use human-interest to make emotional appeals, and its length is determined by the importance of the news from that perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of discourse — narrative, descriptive, expository (or combinations)
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories in method are (1) narrative, (2) descriptive, (3) expository, or (4) any combination of these three forms of discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters may combine narration (series of incidents), description (persons/places), and exposition (causes/motives/results). Narrative features may use fiction devices to sustain interest; exposition should be simple and lucid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of the story — lead and body
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure is concerned with (1) the beginning, or lead, and (2) the body. The informative story usually begins with a summary lead that answers Who? What? Where? When? Why? How? The summary lead includes persons, event, place, time, cause, significant circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any of the elements may be featured in the prominent opening. Feature/entertainment stories often avoid the summary lead and begin unconventionally. In the body, details follow a logical order; repeat only lead details needed for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead content — the 'Five/ Six Ws' and featureing
rubrics_metrics.description: The summary lead includes the following details: (1) the persons, (2) the event, (3) the place, (4) the time, (5) the cause, (6) the significant circumstances. Any one of these elements may be 'featured' in the place of prominence at the beginning of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure essential facts are presented concisely in the lead; choose which element to feature according to news value and reader interest. For features, consider alternative openings that build suspense or scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of the body — logical/chronological order
rubrics_metrics.description: In the body of the story the details follow a logical order. The arrangement in narrative stories is usually chronological.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary repetition of lead material; round out stories in the last paragraph when possible but be aware make-up cuts may truncate endings.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values — questions to determine value and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist for news values: Which paper published it? Paper policy/character? Circulation reach? Appeal to particular class? Point of view favoring that class? Source of interest for average reader? How much would it interest the average reader and why? Was space appropriate? What more significant phases might have been developed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions to judge how newsworthy an item is and whether coverage (space, emphasis) matched its importance; consider audience and paper policy when evaluating slant or prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of news — origin and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions: How did the news originate? Where was the first record made and by whom? What records and persons were consulted? What reference books or material were used to get or verify details? What other possible sources might have been consulted?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate completeness and reliability of sourcing; look for documentary evidence and a diversity of sources; note missed sources that could add verification or context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of news gathering — evidence of how information was obtained
rubrics_metrics.description: What evidence does the story give of the methods by which the news was obtained? Is there any evidence the reporter failed to get important details?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reporting methods (interviews, official records, eyewitnesses) and identify gaps where reporting appears incomplete or one-sided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — fairness, suppression, constructive vs destructive effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story seem fair and unbiased? Is there evidence important facts were suppressed or the story colored to conform to paper policy? Is handling constructive or destructive in effect? What is the constructive purpose of the writer? Does the story tempt the reader to imitate anti-social acts?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge ethical and social effects: fairness, transparency about sources, whether emphasis promotes prevention or sympathy, and avoid sensationalism that panders to morbid curiosity or encourages harmful behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary style — paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze paragraph length and unity: average length, any too long or too short, whether each paragraph is a unit, arrangement and connection of details, effectiveness of paragraph openings to attract the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspaper paragraphs should be comparatively short (typical 35–75 words). Paragraph openings should attract the eye; adjust paragraph starts to improve emphasis and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary style — sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze sentence length and unity: average length, any too long/short, whether construction is evident in rapid reading, unity of expression, firmness of construction, whether sentence-beginnings attract the reader, trailing loose constructions, and variety in length/construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid involved constructions and long periodic sentences; sentences should be unified and clear for rapid reading; vary length for rhythm but keep constructions tight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary style — words and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the style concise or wordy? Is diction original or hackneyed? Is it marked by many adjectives or superlatives? Are verbs specific and forcible? Is diction too learned for the average rapid reader? Are words idiomatic and accurate? Is slang or colloquialism present and what is its effect? Is diction in keeping with tone?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer specific, original wording over colorless general terms and trite phrases; avoid technical/learned words unless fully explained; use slang only when tone justifies it; favor concise diction suited to rapid reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of style — clearness, force, animation, humor, pathos, taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The style of a news story concerns clearness, force, animation, humor, pathos, and taste. Clearness depends on arrangement, connection, and expression of ideas; note brisk movement and steady progress. Humor and pathos may be effective but should avoid ridicule, buffoonery, vulgarity, or violating good taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether style secures intended emotional effects without offense; assess movement and whether opportunities for humor or pathos were developed or left unused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical style and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Peculiarities of abbreviation, capitalization, hyphenation, and use of numerical figures should be noted; each paper has its own typographical style, and consistency must be maintained. Note printing of significant facts in a box, bold-face type, arranging lists of dead and injured, forms for market reports, scores in sports, and similar details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate consistency and appropriateness of typographical devices and whether they give undue prominence or aid comprehension; record house style quirks as part of analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of incident (fires/accidents) stories — important details
rubrics_metrics.description: Important details to consider in analyzing fires and accidents: (1) number of lives lost; (2) number of lives endangered; (3) names of dead and injured; (4) prominent persons and places involved; (5) character and extent of damage; (6) property threatened; (7) cause and responsibility; (8) investigations; (9) preventive measures against recurrence; (10) probable or actual effects; (11) peculiar and unusual circumstances; (12) humorous and pathetic incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any one of these may be the feature of the story and should be played up in the lead according to relative news value; space and prominence are determined by that relative news value.
